content: Clindamycin hydrochloride, when administered vaginally, is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant women. Common side effects include vaginitis, vaginal pain, and diarrhea. Clindamycin vaginal ovules are prescribed for a 3-day treatment course for bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant women. There are no adequate or well-controlled studies of clindamycin vaginal ovules in pregnant women. Diagnostic criteria for bacterial vaginosis include a fishy amine odor when mixed with a 10% potassium hydroxide solution, the presence of clue cells on microscopic examination, and Gram stain findings such as reduced or absent Lactobacillus morphology, a predominance of Gardnerella morphotypes, and few or no white blood cells. Other pathogens commonly associated with vulvovaginitis, such as Trichomonas vaginalis, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Candida albicans, and herpes simplex virus, should be ruled out. Clindamycin vaginal ovules are contraindicated in individuals with a history of hypersensitivity to clindamycin, lincomycin, or any components of the vaginal suppository. They are also contraindicated in individuals with a history of regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis, or antibiotic-associated colitis. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clindamycin, and can range in severity from mild to life-threatening. Oral and parenteral clindamycin has been associated with severe colitis, which can be fatal. Symptoms such as diarrhea, bloody diarrhea, and colitis (including pseudomembranous colitis) have been reported with oral, parenteral, and topical clindamycin formulations. Approximately 30% of the clindamycin dose is systemically absorbed from the vagina, so this diagnosis should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea after using clindamycin vaginal ovules. Treatment with antibacterial agents alters the normal flora of the colon, potentially allowing overgrowth of Clostridium difficile. Studies indicate that a toxin produced by C. difficile is a primary cause of antibiotic-associated colitis. Once pseudomembranous colitis is diagnosed, therapeutic measures should be initiated. Mild cases usually respond to discontinuation of the drug alone, while moderate to severe cases may require fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and treatment with an antibacterial drug effective against C. difficile colitis. Symptoms of pseudomembranous colitis may occur during or after antimicrobial treatment. In clinical trials, 5% of 589 non-pregnant women treated with clindamycin vaginal ovules discontinued therapy due to drug-related adverse events. Other adverse events reported by less than 1% of patients include menstrual disorders, dysuria, pyelonephritis, vaginal discharge, and vaginal infections. Systemic effects such as abdominal cramps, localized abdominal pain, fever, flank pain, headache, and generalized pain have also been reported. Digestive system effects include diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Skin-related effects include rash, pruritus, and application-site reactions. Clindamycin has neuromuscular blocking properties that may enhance the action of other neuromuscular blocking agents, so caution is advised when used concurrently with such agents. In pregnancy, clindamycin vaginal ovules should only be used during the first trimester if clearly needed and if the benefits outweigh the risks. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of clindamycin vaginal ovules in pregnant women during the first trimester. However, systemic administration of clindamycin during the second and third trimesters has not been associated with an increased frequency of congenital abnormalities. Reproductive studies in animals have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, although cleft palates were observed in one mouse strain treated with high doses of clindamycin. This effect was not observed in other mouse strains or species, suggesting it may be strain-specific. Clindamycin has been detected in human milk following oral or parenteral administration. It is unknown if clindamycin is excreted in human milk following vaginal administration. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. The safety and efficacy of clindamycin vaginal ovules in post-menarcheal females have been established based on extrapolation of clinical trial data from adult women. However, the safety and efficacy in pre-menarcheal females have not been established. Clinical studies did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and over to determine whether they respond differently from younger subjects. Clindamycin primarily exerts a bacteriostatic effect by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. It binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit of the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting ribosomal translocation in a manner similar to macrolides. Structural studies of clindamycin bound to ribosomes have been conducted using X-ray crystallography. Clindamycin vaginal ovules are supplied in cartons containing three suppositories with one applicator. They should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F).
